claims.evidence: This is observed by comparing the Tra1 structure in this study with the previously reported structure.

claims.claim: Tra1 contains a large HEAT repeat, followed by the FAT and pseudo-kinase domains.
claims.source: It contains a large HEAT repeat (pink in Figure 2A), followed by the FAT (yellow in Figure 2) and pseudo-kinase domains (jointly also referred to as FATKIN) (cyan in Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Eaf1, Epl1, and Swc4 within the core interact with Tra1 near the FATKIN region.
claims.source: Eaf1, Epl1, and Swc4 within the core (red, green, and purple, respectively, Figures 1 and 2A) interact with Tra1 near the FATKIN region.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figures 1 and 2A.

claims.claim: Eaf1 contributes 5500 Å2 of the total 7700 Å2 buried surface area between the core and Tra1.
claims.source: Of these, Eaf1 is the primary Tra1 interaction partner, contributing 5500 Å2 of the total 7700 Å2 buried surface area between the core and Tra1 (Figure 2B, C).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the structural data and shown in Figure 2B, C.

claims.claim: Arp4 and Act1 are the only components of the core that do not contact Tra1.
claims.source: Arp4 and Act1 (orange and blue, respectively, Figures 1 and 2A) are the only components of the core that do not contact Tra1 (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and contact area calculations shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The NuA4 core can be seen as containing a beta-cluster, a helical bundle, an Arp module, and two Eaf1 extensions.
claims.source: Structurally, the NuA4 core made of Eaf1, Epl1, Swc4, Arp4, and Act1, can be seen as containing a beta-cluster, a helical bundle, an Arp module, and two Eaf1 extensions (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The beta cluster is composed of β-strands from Eaf1 and Epl1.
claims.source: The beta cluster is composed of β-strands from Eaf1 and Epl1 (Figure 2A, oval 1) and sits at the center of the core, surrounded by the helical bundle, Arp module and the Tra1 FAT domain.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The helical bundle contains helices from Eaf1, Epl1, and Swc4.
claims.source: The helical bundle contains helices from Eaf1, Epl1, and Swc4 (Figure 2A, oval 2) and buttresses the interface of the Tra1 FAT and pseudo-kinase domains.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The ARP module is made up of Act1, Arp4, the HSA helix of Eaf1, and Swc4.
claims.source: The largest part of the core is the ARP module, which is made up of Act1, Arp4, the HSA helix of Eaf1, and Swc4 (Figure 2A, oval 3).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Act1 and Arp4 bind to each other end to end to form a tight dimer.
claims.source: Act1 and Arp4 bind to each other, end to end, to form a tight dimer.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claims.claim: The Swc4 ring wraps around the Act1/Arp4 dimer.
claims.source: The Swc4 ring, which includes the SANT domain and a long-extended coil, wraps around this Act1/Arp4 dimer
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claims.claim: The long HSA helix of Eaf1 binds across the Arp4/Act1 dimer.
claims.source: while the long HSA (helicase-SANT-associated) helix of Eaf1 binds across the Arp4/Act1 dimer (similar to other HSA–Arp–actin interactions) (Schubert et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and is similar to other known HSA-Arp-actin interactions.

claims.claim: The role of Eaf1 as a scaffolding subunit within NuA4 is in good agreement with previous genetic and biochemical studies.
claims.source: The role of Eaf1 as a scaffolding subunit within NuA4 is in good agreement with previous genetic and biochemical studies that show that its deletion results in loss of NuA4 complex assembly (Auger et al., 2008; Mitchell et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data in this study and previous studies cited.

claims.claim: Deletion of Eaf1 results in loss of NuA4 complex assembly.
claims.source: The role of Eaf1 as a scaffolding subunit within NuA4 is in good agreement with previous genetic and biochemical studies that show that its deletion results in loss of NuA4 complex assembly (Auger et al., 2008; Mitchell et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: The HAT, TINTIN modules and Yaf9 subunit are flexibly tethered to the core through Epl1, Eaf1, and Swc4, respectively.
claims.source: These missing parts are flexibly tethered to the core through Epl1, Eaf1, and Swc4, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing flexible linkers and the lack of resolved density for these modules.

claims.claim: The HAT module is composed of Yng2, Eaf6, and Esa1, as well as residues 121–400 of Epl1.
claims.source: Reconstitution experiments and the crystal structure of the HAT module show that it is composed of Yng2, Eaf6, and Esa1, as well as residues 121–400 of Epl1 (Xu et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: The segment of Epl1 in the HAT module is connected to the rest of the protein in the core via a poorly conserved and predicted unstructured region of about 90 amino acids.
claims.source: This segment of Epl1 is connected to the rest of the protein in the core of NuA4 via a poorly conserved and predicted unstructured region of about 90 amino acids (residues 400–487) (Figure 3B), in agreement with the lack of a fixed position for the HAT module with respect to the core.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from sequence analysis and the structural data showing flexibility of the HAT module.

claims.claim: The N-terminus of the region of Epl1 integrated into the core is located near the FAT domain of Tra1.
claims.source: The N-terminus of the region of Epl1 integrated into the core is located near the FAT domain of Tra1, making the HAT module a likely candidate for the diffuse density we see in our structure above the FAT domain (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The AlphaFold2 prediction of the NuA4 TINTIN module shows it is split into three main ordered segments.
claims.source: The resulting structure shows the module is split into three main ordered segments: the Eaf3 chromodomain, the Eaf3 MRG/Eaf5 C-term/Eaf7, and the Eaf5 N-term/Eaf1 (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on AlphaFold2 prediction shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The three parts of the TINTIN module appear interconnected through flexible linkers.
claims.source: These three parts appear interconnected through flexible linkers, making the TINTIN module highly extended.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the AlphaFold2 prediction and CX-MS data.

claims.claim: The CX-MS data show crosslinks within each of the three parts of TINTIN but no crosslinks between them.
claims.source: This feature is also captured in the CX-MS data (Setiaputra et al., 2018), which shows crosslinks within each of these three parts but no crosslinks between them (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the CX-MS data mapped on the AlphaFold2 prediction shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The interactions between the Eaf3 MRG and Eaf7 are structurally similar to those in the human homolog.
claims.source: The interactions between the Eaf3 MRG and Eaf7 are structurally similar to those in the human homolog (Xie et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is observed by comparing the AlphaFold2 prediction with the known structure of the human homolog.

claims.claim: The TINTIN module is connected to the NuA4 core through the interaction of the N-termini of Eaf5 and Eaf1.
claims.source: The TINTIN module is connected to the NuA4 core through the interaction of the N-termini of Eaf5 (aa 1–139) and Eaf1 (aa 28–91).
claims.evidence: This is based on the AlphaFold2 prediction and CX-MS data.

claims.claim: The region of Eaf1 that interacts with the TINTIN module is separated from the Eaf1 region in the core by approximately 130 amino acids predicted to be unstructured.
claims.source: The region of Eaf1 that interacts with the TINTIN module is separated from the Eaf1 region located within the core of NuA4 by a segment of approximately 130 amino acids that is predicted to be unstructured (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from sequence analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Yaf9 interacts with the C-terminus of Swc4 (residues 359–476).
claims.source: Finally, CX-MS data show that Yaf9 interacts with the C-terminus of Swc4 (residues 359–476) (Setiaputra et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established from CX-MS data cited.

claims.claim: The YEATs domain of Yaf9 is capable of binding acetylated lysine residues, with the highest affinity for H3K27ac.
claims.source: Previous binding studies have shown that the YEATs domain of Yaf9 is capable of binding acetylated lysine residues, with the highest affinity for H3K27ac (Klein et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: The AlphaFold2 prediction shows that Swc4 binds the Yaf9 β-sandwich on the opposite side of the histone-binding face.
claims.source: The AlphaFold2 prediction of Yaf9 and the C-terminus of Swc4 shows that the Swc4 binds the Yaf9 β-sandwich on the opposite side of the histone-binding face and forms a coil–coil structure with a protruding C-terminal helix on Yaf9 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on AlphaFold2 prediction shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The region of Swc4 integrated into the core and interacting with Yaf9 is linked via a poorly conserved and predicted unstructured region of about 20 amino acids.
claims.source: The region of Swc4 that is integrated into the core of NuA4 and interacts with Yaf9 is linked via a poorly conserved and predicted unstructured region of about 20 amino acids (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from sequence analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: SAGA has been reported to have similar flexible domains to NuA4.
claims.source: SAGA, the other major multisubunit HAT in yeast, has been reported to have similar flexible domains (Setiaputra et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: The flexible regions of NuA4 appear to be more diffuse than the HAT and DUB modules of SAGA.
claims.source: The negative strain structures show that the flexible regions of NuA4 appear to be more diffuse (lower occupancy) than the HAT and DUB modules of SAGA, and are more similar to what is seen as corresponding to the Spt8 subunit (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, C; Setiaputra et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the negative stain EM structures shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: NuA4 and SAGA both contain the activator targeting Tra1 subunit and have a similar overall architecture.
claims.source: Due to the similarities between NuA4 and SAGA, both containing the activator targeting Tra1 subunit and having a similar overall architecture that includes flexible attachment of chromatin-binding and modifying modules, we propose that these two HAT complexes are likely to have a similar chromatin targeting mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarities observed between NuA4 and SAGA.

claims.claim: NuA4 and SAGA are likely to have a similar chromatin targeting mechanism.
claims.source: Due to the similarities between NuA4 and SAGA, both containing the activator targeting Tra1 subunit and having a similar overall architecture that includes flexible attachment of chromatin-binding and modifying modules, we propose that these two HAT complexes are likely to have a similar chromatin targeting mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the structural similarities observed.

claims.claim: The HAT module contains three putative chromatin interacting domains: a chromodomain and the HAT domain in Esa1, and a PHD in Yng2.
claims.source: The HAT module contains three putative chromatin interacting domains: a chromodomain and the HAT domain in Esa1 (the later combines a zinc-finger and MOZ-type HAT domain), and a PHD in Yng2.
claims.evidence: This is based on domain analysis and previous studies.

claims.claim: The PHD domain of Yng2 can bind H3K4me3.
claims.source: Previous reports have shown that the PHD domain of Yng2 can bind H3K4me3, while the HAT domain binds the histone octamer surface of the nucleosome (Xu et al., 2016; Steunou et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: The HAT domain of Esa1 binds the histone octamer surface of the nucleosome.
claims.source: Previous reports have shown that the PHD domain of Yng2 can bind H3K4me3, while the HAT domain binds the histone octamer surface of the nucleosome (Xu et al., 2016; Steunou et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: The HAT module shows increasing affinity for nucleosomes with a greater number of methyl groups on H3K4.
claims.source: Although we did see increasing HAT module affinity for nucleosomes with a greater number of methyl groups on H3K4, affinity for nucleosomes containing both H3K4me3 and acetylation marks on H3 (K9, K14, and K18) demonstrated ~3× binding preference over H3K4me3 alone (Figure 3D, Figure 3, Figure 4 and Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the dCypher binding assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Affinity for nucleosomes containing both H3K4me3 and acetylation marks on H3 demonstrated ~3× binding preference over H3K4me3 alone.
claims.source: Although we did see increasing HAT module affinity for nucleosomes with a greater number of methyl groups on H3K4, affinity for nucleosomes containing both H3K4me3 and acetylation marks on H3 (K9, K14, and K18) demonstrated ~3× binding preference over H3K4me3 alone (Figure 3D, Figure 3, Figure 4 and Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the dCypher binding assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Tetra-acetylated H3 nucleosomes as well as singly acetylated K9, K14, and K18 nucleosomes were not bound by the HAT module.
claims.source: Tetra-acetylated H3 nucleosomes (K4, K9, K14, and K18) as well as singly acetylated K9, K14, and K18 nucleosomes were not bound by the HAT module, indicating that acetylation on its own is poorly or not recognized (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the dCypher binding assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Acetylated lysines likely reduce overall interactions between the histone tails and DNA, allowing the tails greater accessibility.
claims.source: Instead, the acetylated lysines are likely to reduce overall interactions between the histone tails and DNA, allowing the tails greater accessibility by the HAT module of the H3K4me3 mark (Morrison et al., 2018; Marunde et al., 2022a; Morgan et al., 2021; Jain et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the binding data and supported by previous studies cited.

claims.claim: The only predicted chromatin interacting domain within the TINTIN module is the Eaf3 chromodomain.
claims.source: Within the TINTIN module, the only predicted chromatin interacting domain is the Eaf3 chromodomain.
claims.evidence: This is based on domain analysis.

claims.claim: Eaf3 is present in the yeast HDAC RPD3S, where it has been proposed to recognize H3K36me3 modified nucleosomes.
claims.source: Eaf3 is also present in the yeast HDAC RPD3S, where it has been proposed to recognize H3K36me3 modified nucleosomes (Huh et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2013; Ruan et al., 2015; Keogh et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: TINTIN has overall weak affinity for nucleosomes and no specificity for H3K36me3.
claims.source: However, we found that TINTIN has overall weak affinity for nucleosomes and no specificity for H3K36me3, an observations made by others for NuA4 as a whole (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 5B; Li et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the dCypher binding assay data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 5B.

claims.claim: The only slight preference of TINTIN appears to be for H2A and H4 acetylated nucleosomes.
claims.source: The only slight preference of the complex appears to be for H2A and H4 acetylated nucleosomes, though with the caveat that this was observed under conditions of high binding background (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the dCypher binding assay data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 5B.

claims.claim: H2A and H4 histone modifications are made by the HAT module of NuA4.
claims.source: Interestingly, these two sets of histone modifications are made by the HAT module of NuA4.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about NuA4 HAT module function.

claims.claim: NuA4 prefers H3K4me3-containing nucleosomes that are hyperacetylated on H3.
claims.source: Our binding studies show that NuA4 prefers H3K4me3-containing nucleosomes that are hyperacetylated on H3.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the dCypher binding assay data.

claims.claim: Acetylation of H3 in yeast is largely conferred by SAGA, both in the context of transcription and double strand break repair.
claims.source: Acetylation of H3 in yeast is largely conferred by SAGA, both in the context of transcription and double strand break repair (Grant et al., 1997; Kuo et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: NuA4 activity likely follows that of SAGA.
claims.source: Thus, our binding studies suggest that NuA4 activity likely follow that of SAGA, while it would precede the recruitment of factors like TFIID or SWR1 that contain reader modules for H4 acetylation (Matangkasombut and Buratowski, 2003; Ladurner et al., 2003; Durant and Pugh, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the binding studies and the known functions of SAGA and NuA4.

claims.claim: NuA4 activity would precede the recruitment of factors like TFIID or SWR1 that contain reader modules for H4 acetylation.
claims.source: Thus, our binding studies suggest that NuA4 activity likely follow that of SAGA, while it would precede the recruitment of factors like TFIID or SWR1 that contain reader modules for H4 acetylation (Matangkasombut and Buratowski, 2003; Ladurner et al., 2003; Durant and Pugh, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the binding studies and the known functions of these factors.

claims.claim: Many of the components of yeast NuA4 are shared with other complexes.
claims.source: Many of the components of yeast NuA4 are shared with other complexes (Figure 4A; Doyon and Côté, 2004; Grant et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge shown in Figure 4A and supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Part of the ARP module is found in the SWR1 and INO80 chromatin remodelers.
claims.source: Part of the ARP module is also found in the SWR1 and INO80 chromatin remodelers (Mizuguchi et al., 2004; Shen et al., 2000)
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: The large activator targeting Tra1 subunit is shared with SAGA.
claims.source: while the large activator targeting Tra1 subunit is shared with SAGA, the other major HAT with functions in transcription (Grant et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: The HAT and TINTIN can exist outside of NuA4.
claims.source: The HAT and TINTIN can also exist outside of NuA4 (Boudreault et al., 2003; Rossetto et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: The higher eukaryotic TIP60 complex combines components from the yeast NuA4 and SWR1 complexes.
claims.source: Of note, the higher eukaryotic TIP60 complex combines components from the yeast NuA4 and SWR1 complexes (Auger et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: The yeast INO80 and SWR1 complexes function as histone remodelers/histone exchangers during transcription initiation and DNA repair.
claims.source: The yeast INO80 and SWR1 complexes function as histone remodelers/histone exchangers during transcription initiation and DNA repair (Mizuguchi et al., 2004; Shen et al., 2000; Morrison and Shen, 2009; van Attikum et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: These functions of INO80 and SWR1 are in part facilitated by NuA4, which acetylates the nucleosomes that are to be remodeled or have their histones exchanged.
claims.source: These functions are in part facilitated by NuA4, which acetylates the nucleosomes that are to be remodeled or have their histones exchanged (Ranjan et al., 2013; Altaf et al., 2010; Krogan et al., 2004; Downs et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: In SWR1, the ARP module contains Act1, Arp4, Yaf9, and the HSA helix of Swr1 replacing Eaf1.
claims.source: In SWR1, the ARP module contains Act1, Arp4, Yaf9, and the HSA helix of Swr1 replacing Eaf1 (Figure 4B; Wu et al., 2009; Cao et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited and shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: In INO80 the ARP module contains Act1, Arp4, and the HSA helix of Ino80.
claims.source: In INO80 the ARP module contains Act1, Arp4, and the HSA helix of Ino80 (Figure 4B; Knoll et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited and shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: In both SWR1 and INO80, the ARP module is flexible with respect to the core of the complex.
claims.source: In both SWR1 and INO80, the ARP module is flexible with respect to the core of the complex, with the HSA helix of Swr1 and Ino80 predicted to be solvent exposed (Knoll et al., 2018; Brahma et al., 2018; Willhoft et al., 2018; Ayala et al., 2018; Eustermann et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: The solvent exposed side of the HSA helix in INO80 seems to bind extranucleosomal DNA.
claims.source: From biochemical studies, the solvent exposed side of the HSA helix in INO80 seems to bind extranucleosomal DNA, as also predicted for SWR1 (Knoll et al., 2018; Brahma et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: In NuA4, the ARP module surface with the HSA helix is buried in the core of the complex, where it appears to serve largely a structural role.
claims.source: In contrast, in NuA4, the ARP module surface with the HSA helix is buried in the core of the complex, where it appears to serve largely a structural role (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: In S. cerevisiae the multisubunit NuA4 and SAGA acetyltransferase complexes both include the Tra1 transactivation-binding protein.
claims.source: In S. cerevisiae the multisubunit NuA4 and SAGA acetyltransferase complexes both include the Tra1 transactivation-binding protein (Allard et al., 1999; Grant et al., 1998)
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: NuA4 and SAGA do not share any other subunits besides Tra1.
claims.source: In S. cerevisiae the multisubunit NuA4 and SAGA acetyltransferase complexes both include the Tra1 transactivation-binding protein (Allard et al., 1999; Grant et al., 1998), while they do not share any other subunits and acetylate different histone tails (NuA4 targeting H2A/H4; SAGA targeting H3).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge.

claims.claim: NuA4 targets H2A/H4 while SAGA targets H3 for acetylation.
claims.source: In S. cerevisiae the multisubunit NuA4 and SAGA acetyltransferase complexes both include the Tra1 transactivation-binding protein (Allard et al., 1999; Grant et al., 1998), while they do not share any other subunits and acetylate different histone tails (NuA4 targeting H2A/H4; SAGA targeting H3).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge.

claims.claim: Both NuA4 and SAGA contain a central core that interacts with Tra1, primarily through the FAT domain, and anchors the rest of the functional domains.
claims.source: Despite their compositional and functional differences, both complexes contain a central core that interacts with Tra1, primarily through the FAT domain, and anchors the rest of the functional domains.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the structures of both complexes.

claims.claim: The NuA4 core contacts Tra1 through an extensive interface involving Eaf1, Swc4, and Epl1.
claims.source: We describe here how the NuA4 core contacts Tra1 through an extensive interface involving Eaf1, Swc4, and Epl1 (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Yeast SAGA has a much smaller Tra1 interface involving Spt20 and Taf12.
claims.source: In contrast, yeast SAGA has a much smaller Tra1 interface involving Spt20 and Taf12 (Figure 4D; Papai et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited and shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The larger interface between Tra1 and the NuA4 core results in a more rigid connection compared with yeast SAGA.
claims.source: The larger interface between Tra1 and the NuA4 core results in a more rigid connection between these two modules compared with yeast SAGA (Figure 4C, D; Papai et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparing the structures of NuA4 and SAGA shown in Figure 4C, D.

claims.claim: The human TIP60 complex encompasses the functionalities of yeast NuA4 and SWR1 complexes.
claims.source: The human TIP60 complex encompasses the functionalities of yeast NuA4 and SWR1 complexes (Doyon and Côté, 2004; Auger et al., 2008)
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: The metazoan EP400 is the key protein responsible for merging the NuA4 and SWR1 complexes in TIP60.
claims.source: with the metazoan EP400 being the key protein responsible for merging the two complexes present in lower eukaryotes (Auger et al., 2008, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claims.claim: A putative organization of the TIP60 complex is proposed based on the domain organization of EP400 and the structures of SWR1 and NuA4.
claims.source: Based on the domain organization of EP400 and the structures of SWR1 and NuA4, we propose a putative organization of the TIP60 complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Willhoft et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on structural data and domain analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The first step of NuA4 recruitment is the binding of site-specific transcription factors capable of interaction with the Tra1 subunit.
claims.source: From our structural and biochemical data, we propose a sequential model of NuA4 recruitment to target nucleosomes (Figure 5). The first step would be the binding of site-specific transcription factors, capable of interaction with the Tra1 subunit to recruit NuA4.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the structural and biochemical data and shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The NuA4 flexible HAT and reader modules would be able to select neighboring nucleosomes containing preferred modifications after recruitment.
claims.source: The NuA4 flexible HAT and reader modules (TINTIN and Yaf9) would then be able to select neighboring nucleosomes containing preferred modifications, such as H3K4me3 with acetyl groups on H3 K9, K14, and K18.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the structural and biochemical data.

claims.claim: Once a nucleosome is selected by the complex, the HAT module would acetylate histones H2A and H4.
claims.source: Once a nucleosome is selected by the complex, the HAT module would acetylate histones H2A and H4.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the known function of the HAT module.

claims.claim: The NuA4 mechanism of recruitment is likely similar for the human TIP60 homolog.
claims.source: This NuA4 mechanism of recruitment is likely similar for the human TIP60 homolog and may also be shared by other HAT complexes such as SAGA and CBP/p300.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the structural similarities between NuA4 and TIP60.

claims.claim: The NuA4 mechanism of recruitment may be shared by other HAT complexes such as SAGA and CBP/p300.
claims.source: This NuA4 mechanism of recruitment is likely similar for the human TIP60 homolog and may also be shared by other HAT complexes such as SAGA and CBP/p300.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the structural similarities between these HAT complexes.

claims.claim: SAGA and CBP/p300 have their activator-binding and HAT components flexibly separated like NuA4.
claims.source: Like NuA4, SAGA, and CBP/p300 also have their activator-binding and HAT components flexibly separated (Papai et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Fuxreiter et al., 2008; Dyson and Wright, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies cited.

claims.claim: The structural arrangement of HAT complexes likely allows them to target specifically modified nucleosomes within the neighboring chromatin environment.
claims.source: This structural arrangement likely means that recruitment of the complexes does not constrain the HAT module to act on a specific nucleosome, such as the most adjacent one, but could allow for the complex to target specifically modified nucleosomes within the neighboring chromatin environment.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the structural data showing flexible attachment of HAT modules.

results.result: The authors determined a 3.1-Å resolution cryo-EM structure of the NuA4 central hub containing Tra1, Eaf1, Epl1, Swc4, Arp4, and Act1. The structure was validated by crosslinking mass spectrometry data, with all 82 identified crosslinks falling within the 30-Å cutoff for DSS crosslinks.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C35-C38, and C43 collectively demonstrate a well-resolved structure with appropriate validation. The 3.1-Å resolution is supported by standard cryo-EM processing (C37), subunit identification is confirmed by multiple methods including SDS-PAGE, mass spectrometry, and mass photometry (C35), and the structure is validated by compatibility with independent CX-MS data (C43). The methods are rigorous and the resolution is sufficient for the conclusions drawn.

results.result: The rigid central hub of NuA4 contains Tra1, Eaf1, Swc4, Arp4, Act1, and the C-terminus of Epl1, while the HAT module, TINTIN module, and Yaf9 are flexibly attached and appear as diffuse density in the cryo-EM map.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C30, C38-C39, C41-C42 are well-supported by the cryo-EM data showing resolved density for the hub subunits and diffuse density for flexible modules. The distinction between rigid and flexible regions is consistent with the resolution differences observed in the maps and the known nucleosome-interacting functions of the missing modules (C39-C40). This represents a key architectural finding.

results.result: Eaf1 functions as the primary scaffolding factor in NuA4, contributing 5500 Å² of the 7700 Å² buried surface area with Tra1 and providing the conserved HSA helix to the Arp module.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C48, and C57 are supported by structural data showing extensive Eaf1 interactions and buried surface area calculations (C48). The scaffolding role is consistent with previous genetic studies showing that Eaf1 deletion results in loss of complex assembly (C57-C58), providing independent validation of the structural findings.

results.result: The HAT and TINTIN modules are flexibly tethered to the core through unstructured linker regions in Epl1 (~90 amino acids) and Eaf1 (~130 amino acids), respectively, while Yaf9 is connected via Swc4 (~20 amino acids).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C8, C10, C59, C61, C68, and C72 are supported by sequence analysis showing poorly conserved, predicted unstructured regions connecting the modules to the core, consistent with the observed flexibility in cryo-EM maps. The linker lengths are sufficient to explain the observed diffuse density and crosslinking patterns. However, the unstructured nature is predicted rather than directly observed.

results.result: The HAT module preferentially binds nucleosomes containing both H3K4me3 and hyperacetylated H3 tails (K9, K14, K18), showing ~3× higher affinity compared to H3K4me3 alone, while acetylation alone is not recognized.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C31, C80-C82 are supported by dCypher binding assay data (Figure 3D) showing clear binding preferences. The ~3× preference is quantified and the lack of binding to acetylation-only nucleosomes provides important specificity information. The assays were performed in duplicate, though additional replicates would strengthen the conclusions. The interpretation that acetylation increases H3K4me3 accessibility (C83) is reasonable but inferential.

results.result: The TINTIN module shows weak overall affinity for nucleosomes with no specificity for H3K36me3, but slight preference for H2A and H4 acetylated nucleosomes, though this was observed under high background conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C33, C86-C87 are based on dCypher assays (Figure 3E), but the authors explicitly note high binding background as a caveat (C87). The weak affinity and lack of H3K36me3 specificity contradicts expectations from the Eaf3 chromodomain's role in RPD3S (C85), raising questions about whether the TINTIN module is properly folded or whether additional factors are required for nucleosome recognition. The uncertainty about assay conditions limits confidence in these conclusions.

results.result: The current NuA4 structure is compatible with crosslinking mass spectrometry data, unlike the previously reported structure by Wang et al. (2018).
results.evaluation: Claims C44 and C29 are supported by direct comparison of CX-MS data mapped onto both structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 7). All 82 crosslinks fall within the 30-Å DSS cutoff in the current structure, while many violated this constraint in the previous model. This provides strong validation of the current structure and identifies specific errors in the prior work.

results.result: The NuA4 core contains four structural elements: a beta-cluster (Eaf1/Epl1 β-strands), a helical bundle (Eaf1/Epl1/Swc4 helices), an Arp module (Act1/Arp4 dimer with Eaf1 HSA helix and Swc4 ring), and two Eaf1 extensions.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C56 describe the detailed architecture of the core based on the 3.1-Å resolution structure. The structural elements are clearly resolved in the cryo-EM density (Figure 2A) and the Act1/Arp4 dimer with HSA helix binding is consistent with known HSA-Arp-actin interactions (C56). The level of detail is appropriate for the resolution achieved.

results.result: AlphaFold2 prediction of the TINTIN module shows three ordered segments (Eaf3 chromodomain, Eaf3 MRG/Eaf5 C-term/Eaf7, and Eaf5 N-term/Eaf1) interconnected by flexible linkers, consistent with CX-MS data showing crosslinks within but not between segments.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67 are supported by AlphaFold2 modeling and validation with CX-MS data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The lack of crosslinks between segments (C65) supports the predicted flexibility. The similarity to human homolog structures (C66) provides additional validation. However, AlphaFold2 predictions should be interpreted cautiously without experimental validation, though the CX-MS consistency is reassuring.

results.result: NuA4 preferentially binds H3K4me3-containing nucleosomes hyperacetylated on H3, suggesting that NuA4 activity follows SAGA (which acetylates H3) and precedes recruitment of factors like TFIID or SWR1 that recognize H4 acetylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 present a sequential model of HAT complex action based on the binding data (C89) and established knowledge about SAGA function (C90). The inference that NuA4 follows SAGA (C91) is logical given the binding preference for H3-acetylated nucleosomes. The prediction that NuA4 precedes TFIID/SWR1 recruitment (C92) is reasonable but remains a model requiring in vivo validation.

results.result: In NuA4, the Arp module HSA helix is buried in the core serving a structural role, contrasting with SWR1 and INO80 where the HSA helix is solvent-exposed and flexible, potentially binding extranucleosomal DNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C104, C100-C102 compare the Arp module organization across complexes. The buried nature of the HSA helix in NuA4 is directly observed in the structure (C104, Figure 4B), while the flexible, solvent-exposed nature in SWR1/INO80 is established from prior studies (C102-C103). This functional distinction is well-supported and highlights how shared modules are adapted for different roles.

results.result: The NuA4 core contacts Tra1 through an extensive interface involving Eaf1, Swc4, and Epl1 (7700 Å² total), resulting in a more rigid connection compared to yeast SAGA, which has a smaller Tra1 interface involving Spt20 and Taf12.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 are supported by structural comparison (Figure 4C-D) and buried surface area calculations. The larger interface in NuA4 (C109) compared to SAGA (C110) logically explains the observed rigidity difference (C111). The comparison is based on published SAGA structures, providing appropriate context for the NuA4 findings.

results.result: The authors propose a sequential model of NuA4 recruitment: (1) Tra1 binds site-specific transcription factors, (2) flexible HAT and reader modules select neighboring nucleosomes with preferred modifications, and (3) the HAT module acetylates H2A and H4.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 present a mechanistic model based on the structural data showing flexible module attachment and the nucleosome binding preferences. The model is logical and consistent with known Tra1 function (C11, C22) and HAT module specificity (C7, C25). However, this remains a proposed model requiring in vivo validation through functional studies. The model is clearly presented as speculative (Figure 5).

results.result: The authors propose that NuA4's recruitment mechanism, involving flexible separation of activator-binding and HAT components, is likely shared by other HAT complexes including SAGA, CBP/p300, and human TIP60.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76, C118-C121 extend the NuA4 model to other HAT complexes based on architectural similarities (C75, C120). While the flexible architecture is established for SAGA and CBP/p300 (C120), the functional implications remain speculative. The proposal that this arrangement allows targeting of specifically modified nucleosomes rather than the most adjacent one (C121) is logical but lacks direct experimental support. This represents an interesting hypothesis requiring further testing.

results.result: A putative organization of the human TIP60 complex is proposed based on EP400 domain organization and the structures of yeast NuA4 and SWR1.
results.evaluation: Claim C114 presents a speculative model for TIP60 organization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) based on domain analysis and structural homology. While the approach is reasonable given that TIP60 combines NuA4 and SWR1 functionalities (C112-C113), this remains a computational prediction without experimental validation. The model provides a useful framework for future studies but should be clearly distinguished from experimentally determined structures.

results.result: Background claims establishing the known functions and composition of NuA4 and related HAT complexes, including that NuA4 acetylates H4 and H2A, contains 13 subunits (~1 MDa), and is organized into four modules (Tra1, core, HAT, TINTIN).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C13-C27 represent established knowledge from prior literature, appropriately cited throughout. These background claims are confirmed by the current study's mass spectrometry (C18-C19) and structural data (C20). The authors accurately represent prior work and provide appropriate context for their findings.

results.result: The authors report a 3.1-Å resolution cryo-EM structure of the NuA4 central hub, identifying the subunits Eaf1, Epl1, Swc4, Arp4, Act1, and Tra1 within this rigid core.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state 'The cryo-EM data are of very high quality, and enable the authors to devise a structural model that is in much better agreement with biochemical data than previously reported models.' This indicates acceptance of the structural resolution and subunit identification claims.

results.result: The structure reveals that the HAT and TINTIN modules, along with Yaf9, are flexibly tethered to the rigid central hub through Epl1, Eaf1, and Swc4, respectively, appearing as diffuse density in the cryo-EM map.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the structural model is 'in much better agreement with biochemical data than previously reported models,' implicitly accepting the flexible architecture claims. No concerns are raised about the interpretation of diffuse density or flexible tethering.

results.result: Eaf1 is identified as the primary scaffolding factor, contributing 5500 Ų of the total 7700 Ų buried surface area between the core and Tra1, and providing the conserved HSA helix to the Arp module.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question the structural analysis or the role of Eaf1 as a scaffolding factor. The high-quality cryo-EM data is praised, supporting the detailed structural claims about Eaf1's interactions.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that all 82 crosslinks from published CX-MS data fall within the 30 Å cutoff when mapped onto their structure, while the previous NuA4 structure was incompatible with this data.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly requests 'XL-MS done on the authors own complex, to further validate their own structure,' indicating that while the mapping of published crosslinks is noted, independent validation is needed. The reviewers want the authors' own crosslinking data rather than relying solely on published data from another group.

results.result: The HAT module shows ~3× binding preference for nucleosomes containing both H3K4me3 and hyperacetylated H3 tails (K9, K14, K18) over H3K4me3 alone, with no binding to tetra-acetylated or singly acetylated nucleosomes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises significant concerns: 'The lack of binding to the tetra acetylated nucleosome is the incorrect control as no binding is shown for the tri-acetylation in the absence of H3K4me3.' They request additional experiments including peptide binding assays and charge substitution mutants to validate the interpretation that acetylation simply liberates the H3 tail. The reviewers state this is 'possibly the most interesting biological conclusions from the manuscript' but require 'further biochemistry...to bolster these modified nucleosome experiments.'

results.result: The TINTIN module shows weak overall affinity for nucleosomes with no specificity for H3K36me3, but slight preference for H2A and H4 acetylated nucleosomes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 requests 'further biochemistry on the TINTIN and HAT nucleosome interaction...to show these interactions outside of the dCypher screen.' The caveat that TINTIN binding was 'observed under conditions of high binding background' is noted in the manuscript, and reviewers want additional validation beyond the dCypher assay.

results.result: The isolated NuA4 complex contains all 13 subunits with a molecular weight of about 1 MDa, confirmed by SDS-PAGE, mass spectrometry, and mass photometry.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly requests 'further characterisation of their sample to confirm it is indeed a single biochemical species as they state. Techniques such as AUC, intact mass spectrometry, or mass photometry approaches could help to answer this question.' While mass photometry data is mentioned in the manuscript, the reviewer wants additional characterization to confirm homogeneity.

results.result: The authors propose a sequential recruitment model where Tra1 recruits NuA4 to genomic sites through transcription factor interactions, then flexible HAT and TINTIN modules select nearby nucleosomes for acetylation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this mechanistic model. The statement that the structure 'represents an important puzzle piece towards a molecular understanding of chromatin modification' suggests acceptance of the proposed recruitment mechanism based on the structural findings.

results.result: The NuA4 core contains structurally distinct regions: a beta-cluster, helical bundle, Arp module, and Eaf1 extensions, with detailed subunit organization including the Act1/Arp4 dimer wrapped by Swc4 and the HSA helix of Eaf1.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praise the high-quality cryo-EM data and do not question the detailed structural organization of the core. The structural model is described as being 'in much better agreement with biochemical data than previously reported models.'

results.result: Comparison with SAGA reveals that NuA4 has a larger Tra1 interface involving Eaf1, Swc4, and Epl1, resulting in a more rigid connection compared to SAGA's smaller interface with Spt20 and Taf12.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the comparative structural analysis between NuA4 and SAGA. The structural comparisons are implicitly accepted as part of the overall high-quality structural work.

results.result: AlphaFold2 predictions show the TINTIN module split into three ordered segments connected by flexible linkers, with connections to the core through Eaf1 and Yaf9 binding to Swc4.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question the AlphaFold2 modeling or the interpretation of TINTIN module organization. The integration of computational predictions with experimental data is implicitly accepted.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate H3K4me3 binding preference claims (C7, C31, C80-C82). OpenEval finds the dCypher data supportive with minor concerns about replicates. Peer reviewers are more critical, questioning the control experiments and requesting additional peptide binding assays and charge substitution mutants to validate the acetylation mechanism interpretation.

Both evaluate TINTIN module nucleosome binding claims (C9, C33, C86-C87). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to high binding background and lack of H3K36me3 specificity. Peer reviewers also express UNCERTAINTY and request additional biochemistry beyond the dCypher screen to validate these interactions.

Both evaluate detailed core architecture claims (C50-C56). OpenEval finds the structural elements well-resolved and appropriate for 3.1-Å resolution. Peer reviewers also support these claims, praising the high-quality cryo-EM data and structural model.

Both evaluate comparative analysis of Arp module organization between NuA4 and SAGA (C109-C111). OpenEval finds the buried surface area calculations and interface comparisons well-supported. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these structural comparisons without raising concerns.

Both address crosslinking validation (C44, C29, C43). OpenEval finds the mapping of published CX-MS data onto the structure strongly supportive. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY and explicitly request new XL-MS experiments on the authors' own complex for independent validation, rather than relying solely on published data.

Both evaluate AlphaFold2 modeling of TINTIN module (C63-C65, C67). OpenEval supports the predictions with cautious interpretation, noting CX-MS validation. Peer reviewers accept the computational modeling integrated with experimental data without raising concerns.

Both evaluate Eaf1 scaffolding role claims (C5-C6, C48). OpenEval finds structural data and buried surface area calculations supportive, with genetic validation. Peer reviewers do not question these claims and praise the high-quality structural analysis.

Both evaluate the mechanistic recruitment model (C115-C117, C11-C12). OpenEval supports the model as logical but notes it requires in vivo validation. Peer reviewers also support the model, describing the structure as 'an important puzzle piece towards a molecular understanding of chromatin modification.'

Both evaluate structural resolution and validation claims (C2, C37-C38). OpenEval finds 3.1-Å resolution well-supported with appropriate validation methods. Peer reviewers explicitly praise 'very high quality' cryo-EM data, supporting these claims. Peer result also includes C4, C30 about flexible modules.

Both address flexible architecture claims. OpenEval evaluates C4, C30, C38-C39, C41-C42 regarding rigid hub and flexible modules as well-supported. Peer reviewers evaluate overlapping claims C3, C36, C39, C41-C42, C59, acknowledging the model is 'in much better agreement with biochemical data' without raising concerns.

Partial overlap on subunit identification (C35). OpenEval evaluates C35 as part of comprehensive structural validation including mass spectrometry and mass photometry. Peer reviewers request additional characterization (AUC, intact mass spectrometry) to confirm sample homogeneity, expressing UNCERTAINTY despite mass photometry data mentioned in manuscript.

Minimal overlap on flexible linker claims (C3, C59). OpenEval evaluates linker predictions as supported by sequence analysis and cryo-EM, noting unstructured nature is predicted rather than directly observed. Peer reviewers implicitly accept flexible architecture without specific concerns about linker predictions.

OpenEval evaluates sequential HAT complex action model (C89-C92), finding it logical based on binding data and established SAGA function, but noting in vivo validation is needed. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific mechanistic sequence.

OpenEval evaluates comparative Arp module organization across NuA4, SWR1, and INO80 complexes (C104, C100-C102), finding the functional distinctions well-supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this cross-complex comparison.

OpenEval evaluates extension of flexible architecture model to other HAT complexes (C75-C76, C118-C121) as UNCERTAIN, noting the hypothesis lacks direct experimental support. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this broader generalization.

OpenEval evaluates speculative TIP60 organization model (C114) as UNCERTAIN, noting it is a computational prediction without experimental validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this TIP60-specific modeling.

OpenEval evaluates background literature claims (C1, C13-C27) as appropriately cited and supported. Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate these established knowledge claims, focusing instead on novel findings.
